title: Solo Bridal Photoshoot: How to Take Wedding Photos Alone — cv.cm
description: How to plan a solo bridal or solo wedding photoshoot: options, checklist, shot list, settings for a white dress, gown poses and a self-shot tripod workflow.
h1: How do you take wedding photos of just one person?
answer: Choose who shoots (a studio, a hired photographer, a friend, or yourself on a tripod), book the hour before sunset or soft shade, and follow a shot list from details to full-length. Meter on the face and add +0.3 to +1 EV so the white dress stays white without losing lace detail. Hold the bouquet at navel height and keep hands soft.

sections.h: What a solo bridal shoot is, and who it is for
body: A solo bridal photoshoot is a session with one person in wedding clothes and no partner in the frame. The reasons are different for everyone, and every one of them is a good reason.

ul: Bridal portraits before the wedding: many brides want calm, unhurried photos of the dress, hair and makeup that the busy wedding day does not allow.
A solo wedding for yourself: in Japan, photo studios offer solo wedding (ソロウェディング) plans for people who want to wear a wedding dress without marrying, and the idea has spread to other countries.
A milestone: a 30th or 40th birthday, recovering from an illness, or starting again after a divorce.
A partner who cannot be there: work abroad, military service, visa delays, or a partner who has died.
Grooms and non-binary people: a solo session in a suit, a traditional robe or any outfit works the same way. The advice on this page is not only for brides.
Second wear: a chance to wear the dress or a traditional outfit again, or to try a style you did not wear on the day.

body: Wedding clothing differs around the world. A white gown is common in many countries, but solo shoots also use a red qipao, an áo dài, a hanbok, a kimono such as a white shiromuku, a kebaya, a lehenga or a saree, or a mix of a gown and a traditional outfit. The planning and camera advice below works for all of them. Where white is mentioned, read it as any very bright fabric.

sections.h: Four ways to do it: studio, photographer, friend, or yourself
body: Pick the option first, because it decides your budget, how much time you have, and how many outfits you can wear.

body: When you book a studio or photographer, ask the same things you would ask for a wedding: how many edited photos are included, whether you get the unedited files, how long the session is, how many outfit changes are allowed, and whether location fees, travel, extra retouching or rush delivery cost more. Get the answers in writing.

body.note: Budget tiers without numbers: a self-shot session costs only what you already own plus perhaps a tripod and a remote. A friend session adds hair and makeup. A hired photographer adds the session fee. A full studio package is the highest because it includes the dress, styling and sets.

body: Start four to eight weeks ahead if you are renting a dress or booking a professional. A self-shot session can be planned in a week.

ol: Date and backup date. Pick a second date for rain or strong wind.

Time of day. Plan to shoot in the last hour before sunset, the first hour after sunrise, or in open shade. Look up sunrise and sunset for your exact place and date with your phone's weather app or an official calculator such as NOAA's Solar Calculator.

Venue and permits. Some parks, gardens, temples, heritage sites and beaches need a permit for photo sessions or do not allow tripods. Check the site's rules before the day. Do not block paths or entrances, and ask before photographing other people.
Outfit fittings. Do the last fitting in the shoes you will wear, because the hem length depends on them.
Hair and makeup. Book a trial. Ask for makeup that is slightly stronger than daily makeup, and avoid heavy sunscreen with a white cast if you plan to use flash.
Accessories: veil, bouquet (real or silk), shoes, jewelry, hair pieces, gloves, a shawl for cold weather.
Transport. A long gown fills a car seat. Bring a clean sheet to sit on and a garment bag.
Weather. A cloudy day is not a problem; it gives soft light. Strong wind is useful for veils but hard for hair.

body: Pack an emergency kit in one bag:

ul: Safety pins, hair clips and bobby pins (also to tighten a loose dress at the back, out of view).
Double-sided fashion tape, a small sewing kit, a lint roller.
Tissues, blotting paper, lipstick and powder for touch-ups.
Water with a straw (keeps lipstick in place), a small snack.
Flat shoes for walking between spots, a light jacket, an umbrella.
A clean white sheet or towel to protect the hem on dirty ground.
Spare camera battery and memory card, or a power bank for a phone.

sections.h: Shot list for a solo bridal session
body: A shot list keeps you moving and makes sure the album has variety: details, full-length, medium and close shots. For a one-hour session, aim for 12 to 15 setups and a few frames of each.

sections.h: Camera and phone settings for a white dress
body: A camera meter tries to make what it sees a middle grey. When a white dress fills a large part of the frame, the meter thinks the scene is too bright and darkens it. The dress turns dull grey and the face looks muddy. The fix is to tell the camera to make the picture brighter, while watching that the brightest part of the dress keeps its detail.

ul: Start with exposure compensation of +0.3 to +1 EV in aperture priority (A or Av). Use the higher end when the dress fills most of the frame or the background is bright.
Meter on the face. Use spot or center-weighted metering on the skin, or face detection, then check the dress.

Turn on the highlight warning (blinkies) or zebras. If large areas of the dress blink, reduce the exposure by 1/3 stop at a time until only small shiny spots blink. Lace and folds must still show texture.
Some Nikon cameras have highlight-weighted metering, which is designed to protect bright areas such as a spot-lit bride's dress.
Shoot RAW if your camera allows it. You can recover a little highlight detail and fix white balance later.
White balance: if the dress looks yellow under indoor bulbs, choose the tungsten preset or set a custom white balance on the dress itself.

body: These are starting points. A Canon wedding article shows a full-length bride by a cloudy-day window shot at +1.7 EV, so do not be afraid of a large correction when the scene is bright. Always check the screen and the highlight warning.

Lens choice: 50 mm and 85 mm (full-frame equivalent) are the classic portrait lengths. On a full-frame camera in vertical orientation, a full-length frame that is about 2 m tall needs roughly 3 m of distance with a 50 mm lens and about 5 m with 85 mm.

On a phone: use the 1x main camera for full-length shots from about 1.5 to 2 m, and 2x or 3x for half-body and close-ups. Avoid the 0.5x ultra-wide close to the body, because it stretches arms and the dress at the edges. Tap the face to focus. If the dress looks blown out, drag the exposure slider down a little. On an iPhone, touch and hold the face until AE/AF Lock appears so the exposure does not jump between frames. Portrait mode blurs the background, but check the edges of the veil, which phones often blur by mistake.

sections.h: Posing in a gown, veil and bouquet
body: A long dress hides the legs, so the shape of the pose comes from the shoulders, arms, waist and the line of the skirt.

ul: Bouquet at navel height or a little lower. Held at the chest, it hides the waist and looks stiff. Tilt it slightly forward so the flowers face the camera.
Elbows away from the body. A small gap between arm and waist shows the shape of the dress and looks slimmer.
Soft hands. Let fingers rest, slightly curved. Do not grip the skirt or bouquet hard; tension shows in the knuckles.
Weight on the back leg, front knee slightly bent. The dress hides the legs, but the hips and shoulders still angle naturally.
Turn the body about 45 degrees to the camera and bring the face back. Chin slightly forward and down.
Fan the train: for front and back shots, spread the train in a smooth curve on the ground. A helper can lift it and let it fall, or you can kick it gently behind you before each frame.
Veil: hold one edge out at arm's length, let the wind carry it, or bring it forward over the face for a close-up.
Walking: lift the front of the skirt a little with one hand so you do not step on it, and walk slower than normal.

body: If you feel awkward, give yourself a small action: adjusting an earring, smelling the bouquet, looking down at the ring, walking and turning. Movement looks more natural than holding still.

sections.h: Handling sun and backlight with a white dress
body: Hard midday sun is the hardest light for a white dress. The dress blows out, the face gets dark eye shadows, and the bride squints. Move into open shade: the shadow of a building or a large tree, with open sky in front of you. The light is soft and even, and the dress keeps its texture.
Backlight at golden hour (the sun behind you, low in the sky) makes the veil and the edges of the dress glow. The camera will make your face dark. Choose one of these fixes:

ol: Add +1 to +1.7 EV and accept a bright, airy background.
Use a white or silver reflector held at waist height in front of you to bounce light back to the face. A friend can hold it, or lean it on a stand or a bag.
Use the phone's HDR (usually automatic) or a camera's fill flash at low power.
Turn it into a silhouette: expose for the sky and keep a clear profile.

body.note: Never look at the sun through a camera viewfinder or point a long lens directly at it. On a mirrorless camera or phone, use the screen and keep the sun just outside the frame or behind your head.

sections.h: Self-shot workflow: a solo wedding with no photographer
body: You can do the whole session alone with a tripod and a remote. It takes more time per frame, so plan fewer setups (8 to 10) and allow two hours.

ol: Set up the tripod at chest or waist height. Waist height makes the body look taller in full-length shots.
Frame the shot with some extra space around you, because you can crop later but cannot add space.
Mark your spot on the ground with a small stone, a hair clip or the toe of your shoe.
Focus: turn on face or eye detection if your camera has it. If not, place a stand-in (a bag or the bouquet on a chair) on your mark, focus on it, then switch to manual focus so the focus stays there.
Use f/4 to f/5.6 for safety. At 3 m with a 50 mm lens on full frame, f/4 keeps about 0.9 m in focus; f/2 keeps only about 0.4 m.

Trigger: use the camera maker's phone app to see the live view and press the shutter from your phone, or a Bluetooth remote hidden in the bouquet. If you only have a timer, set 10 seconds with several frames per press if your camera offers it.

On a phone: set the 3 or 10 second timer, which fires a short burst on many phones. Some phones also start the timer with a raised palm or a voice command. A small Bluetooth remote is cheap and works with most phones.
After every setup, walk back and check sharpness by zooming in on the eyes. Then change one thing: pose, angle or veil.

body: The self-portrait photography guide on this shelf covers tripods, remotes and focusing alone in more detail.
Pick the best 20 to 40 photos. Edit them all in the same way so the set looks like one story.

ul: Whites: lower highlights a little to bring back lace, then raise whites so the dress is clean white, not grey.
White balance: a dress should look white or ivory. If it looks blue in shade, warm it slightly.
Skin: soften blemishes lightly. Heavy smoothing makes the skin look plastic next to the sharp lace.
Crop for the use: 4:5 for social posts, 2:3 or 3:4 for prints, 16:9 for a screen. Straighten horizons and door frames.
Before posting online, remove GPS location from the files, for example with cv.cm's EXIF tool, especially if you shot near your home.
Group details, portraits and wide scenes into a collage or album spread; one large photo and three small detail photos per page works well.

faq.q: Is it strange to have a wedding photoshoot without a partner?
faq.a: No. Solo bridal portraits are a long tradition, and solo wedding plans are offered by photo studios in Japan and elsewhere. People do it to celebrate themselves, a milestone, or a dress they love.

faq.q: How long does a solo bridal photoshoot take?
faq.a: With a photographer, one to two hours is typical for one outfit and two or three locations. Add about an hour for each extra outfit, and allow more time if you are shooting yourself on a tripod.

faq.q: What should I bring to a bridal photoshoot?
faq.a: The dress, veil, shoes, bouquet and jewelry, plus an emergency kit: safety pins, clips, tape, tissues, blotting paper, lipstick, water with a straw, flat shoes and a clean sheet to protect the hem.

faq.q: What is the best time of day for bridal photos?
faq.a: The hour before sunset and the hour after sunrise give soft, warm light that flatters skin and keeps detail in a white dress. If you must shoot at midday, use open shade.

faq.q: Can I take good bridal photos with a phone?
faq.a: Yes. Use the 1x lens for full-length shots and 2x or 3x for close-ups, tap and lock focus on the face, lower the exposure slider if the dress loses detail, and use a tripod with the timer if you are alone.

faq.q: Can a groom do a solo wedding photoshoot?
faq.a: Yes. Everything here works for a suit or a traditional outfit. A dark suit is the opposite problem of a white dress: if it fills the frame, you may need to reduce exposure so it does not turn grey.
